study: 6-model story-angle quality round-robin — Fable 5.1 vs Opus 5 vs Fable 5 vs Opus 4.8 vs Sonnet 5 vs Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 (meanest-editor) blind judge
note: Reconstructed from on-disk verdict files by collect.py. One record per judgment; ordering encodes which model sat in slot A vs B.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four cleaner, sellable lanes instead of making compliance do too much work. Its pricing angle, "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm," is risky but properly fenced with the proof a reporter would demand; B just kills the nearby idea as "hallucinated_fact," which leaves a real Enterprise-pricing hook on the floor. B's strongest line, "How Notion made a shared editor work with no connection at all," is sharper than A's offline contrarian take, but one safer technical angle does not beat A's broader strategic map.
gaps_in_A: "Notion shipping offline mode in 2026 is an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" overstates a feature launch into a corporate confession; the facts do not prove Notion reversed a belief.
"cutting against the security-upsell norm" needs competitor evidence and precise pricing scope; the update only says no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans.
"as sovereignty demands spread" is plausible context, but it is still a trend claim without a supplied regulatory peg or outside proof.
gaps_in_B: "bank and hospital compliance" invents hospitals; the update says healthcare buyers generally and gives zero healthcare customers.
"The regulated-buyer category is the protagonist" is doing cleanup duty for a padded angle that overlaps heavily with the bank and residency stories.
"Notion ships enterprise security without the security tax" marked as `hallucinated_fact` is over-refusal; a narrower existing-Enterprise no-price-change pricing angle is in the facts.
"It just shipped the checklist" is lazy shorthand for three distinct controls and reads like launch copy, not a reporter's story.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it does the boring adult thing: it turns the supplied facts into four usable beats without inventing a little movie around them. Its strongest headline, "Four of the five largest US banks are piloting Notion — after it agreed to hand over the keys," is sharp but still anchored in the update; B's "The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" invents a singular bank, a prior ban, and a scene the facts do not support. B has the best technical security angle in "Who holds the keys," but one strong angle does not launder invented drama elsewhere.
gaps_in_A: "Notion shipping offline mode in 2026 is an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" overstates motive. The update supports offline mode shipping; it does not support Notion admitting anything.

"sovereignty demands spread" is plausible context, but it needs a named rule, enforcement moment, or buyer mandate. A flags that proof later, but the headline still leans on an external trend not in the update.
"cutting against the security-upsell norm" is a good angle only if competitor pricing proof exists. A correctly asks for it, but the claim is still doing work before the evidence is in.

A underuses the technical security story. "customer-managed keys via AWS KMS" raises concrete questions about what Notion can still access, key revocation, backups, logs, and telemetry; A mostly turns that into pricing and procurement.
gaps_in_B: "The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" is invented. The facts say regulated buyers previously could not adopt and four of five top US banks run pilots; they do not say one bank banned staff use.

"A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" is a clever line with no evidentiary spine. Nothing in the update says Notion dismissed offline for a decade.

"Notion against Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace" imports a competitive war frame the update never supplied. That may be true market context, but it needs evidence before it becomes the protagonist.

"at least one bank, insurer, or healthcare provider" drifts beyond the facts. Healthcare is only a company assertion and insurer is not in the update; this is how a decent angle starts picking up hitchhikers.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the facts and finds four genuinely usable doors into the story. Its strongest move is "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm" because that uses a real supplied fact and asks for the missing proof before getting cocky. B can write, but "Notion's compliance stack puts Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive in regulated enterprise" names a competitive fight the update never gave it. That is how a founder ends up pitching a story the proof packet cannot survive.
gaps_in_A: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is punchy but imprecise. Customers hold their own keys via AWS KMS; Notion did not literally hand keys to banks.

"Notion shipping offline mode in 2026 is an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" overstates the confession. The update supports an architecture tension, not an admission unless Notion will say why buyers rejected online-only.
"security-upsell norm" and the "SSO tax" contrast need outside competitor proof. A correctly asks for it, but the angle should not leave the building until that comparison is sourced.
gaps_in_B: "anchored in named institutions" is wrong. The update says four of the five largest US banks run pilots, but no bank is named.
"Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive" invents a named competitive war. The facts do not show displacement, RFP wins, or that Microsoft and Atlassian are newly exposed.
"secure facilities" and "air-gap scenarios" drag the offline angle into unsupported territory. The fact is no-connection editing that syncs on reconnect, not air-gapped deployment.

"pilot-eligible" to "procurement-approvable" is consultant fog. Pilots are not proof of procurement approval, and this category angle mostly repackages the bank and compliance angles with a fancier hat.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds four real doors into the story without pretending the facts are stronger than they are. Its pricing angle, "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices," is the kind of sharp business-model read a founder can actually pitch. B has good instincts, but "Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents a competitive displacement story before the evidence earns it. That is how a decent angle turns into a reporter's follow-up question with teeth.
gaps_in_A: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is a little too causal and cute; the update says customers can hold keys via AWS KMS, not that the bank pilots happened because of that concession.
"the prevailing belief: modern cloud collaboration tools treat offline as a legacy concern" needs outside proof before it becomes the spine of a contrarian pitch.
The sovereignty angle needs one external peg or named regulatory requirement; A asks for it, but without it this is still a launch-adjacent trend read.
gaps_in_B: "quietly testing Notion" invents tone. The update says the banks run pilots; it does not say quiet, stealthy, leaked, or reluctant.
"clearing bars historically reserved for purpose-built regulated-industry software" overstates the facts. Pilots are not clearance, adoption, or compliance blessing.
"Notion is angling for accounts that used to belong to compliance-hardened incumbents" invents incumbents, replacement, and competitive threat without a single named vendor or displacement fact.
B misses two of the cleanest available angles: offline-first as an architectural reversal and no pricing change as a security-upsell/pricing story. Those are better than the padded incumbent angle.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it keeps the good press shapes and throws the hand grenades back over the fence instead of carrying them into the pitch. A keeps an invented contrarian line — "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" — which is exactly the sort of clever-sounding overreach that gets murdered in a reporter's inbox. B's strongest sentence is its discipline: "Without a bank willing to be identified, this becomes a claim the reporter cannot check and the angle should be shelved." That is useful PR judgment, not decoration.
gaps_in_A: "Notion against Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace" imports a competitive fight the update did not supply. It may be true in the world, but it is not grounded in this brief.

"The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" invents a cleaner before/after than the facts support. The update says regulated buyers previously could not adopt and four top banks run pilots; it does not prove the same bank banned use and then reversed course.

"A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" is the big sin: a neat contrarian headline built on an unsupplied claim about Notion's history and SaaS ideology.

"compliance features are usually a paid tier" and "arrive inside the existing Enterprise plan" overstate the pricing fact. The brief only says no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans, not that every new control is bundled for all buyers.
gaps_in_B: "Notion's 100 million users could not get it past bank and hospital compliance" is too broad. The bank proof is supplied; the hospital proof is not.
"It just shipped the checklist" makes the controls sound complete before the proof is in. Residency, processing, backups, telemetry, local offline cache, and key custody still need hard answers.
"Story type: exec-spotlight" is the wrong label for the offline angle. The facts support an engineering deep dive, not an executive profile.

B leaves the pricing fact underused. It rightly refuses "security tax," but a narrower angle around "no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans" could survive with competitor pricing proof and careful caveats.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it knows where the bodies are buried: the bank-pilot claim is powerful but fragile, and A keeps hammering the proof before letting the founder swan into a reporter's inbox. Its best angle, "Who holds the keys: what customer-managed encryption actually protects against," is a real security story, not a feature brochure. B has useful shapes, but "The Notion can't do enterprise objection now has a rebuttal anchored in named institutions" invents named institutions the update does not provide. That's not strategy; that's stepping on a rake in dress shoes.
gaps_in_A: "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" invents the decade of dismissal. The update says offline-first shipped; it does not say Notion dismissed offline.
"The bank that wouldn't let its staff use Notion is now piloting it" makes an unnamed pilot sound like a named buyer with a prior ban. Good instinct, too much theater.
"sovereignty as an upsell is standard practice across enterprise software" may be true, but it is not in the facts. A correctly asks for proof, but the angle leans on the claim before earning it.
A refuses "Data residency arrives for European customers" as a duplicate and misses the cleaner EU/Australia data-sovereignty policy lens. That lens exists; it just needs not to be inflated.
gaps_in_B: "anchored in named institutions" is flatly unsupported. The update gives a count of bank pilots, not names.
"Notion's compliance stack puts Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive" imports competitors and declares them threatened before showing displacement, RFP wins, or switching evidence.
"forced to localize data for Europe and Australia" invents regulatory coercion. The facts say Notion added data residency options; they do not prove it was forced.
"secure facilities" and "air-gap scenarios" drag in use cases the update does not support. Offline editing is not the same story as air-gapped enterprise computing.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it separates the real beats instead of squeezing the bank claim until it squeaks: "Who holds the keys: what customer-managed encryption actually protects against" is a security story that can stand even if the bank names do not. B has competent shapes, but "Four of the five largest US banks are quietly testing Notion" leans on a fragile, unnamed customer claim and adds drama the update did not supply. gaps_in_A: "A cloud-native workspace is rebuilding for the offline case it spent a decade dismissing" imports a decade-long Notion attitude the update never gave you.

"historically seen as too lightweight" and "consumer-rooted software" import market baggage not present in the update.

"Notion lets EU and Australian enterprise customers keep their data at home" overstates data residency before proving what is covered: backups, logs, telemetry, support access, and derived data all matter.

Refusing "Notion ships offline-first editing" as "a bare feature description" misses the real engineering/local-first angle: offline edit plus sync-on-reconnect at roughly 100M-user scale is not just a feature blurb.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it refuses the seductive fake thesis and replaces it with a cleaner, reportable engineering angle. A keeps 'The cloud-only collaboration tool just added offline editing and customer-held keys — a reversal worth examining,' which leans on an orthodoxy the update does not prove; B gives us 'How Notion made a shared editor work with no connection at all,' with a protagonist and proof a reporter can actually ask for. That is the difference between strategy and a clever sentence looking for evidence.
gaps_in_A: 'The cloud-only collaboration tool' and 'a reversal worth examining' are not established by the update; A needs proof of Notion's prior architecture and the alleged reversal before this belongs in the kept set.
'The prevailing belief is that always-online, vendor-managed cloud is the whole point' invents an industry premise, then builds a contrarian angle on it. Nice trap, bad footing.

'Notion bets regulated finance and healthcare buyers will pay for control, not features' overclaims buyer motivation and pricing. The facts say no pricing change for existing Enterprise plans, not that buyers will pay for control over features.

'How Notion made a shared editor work with no connection at all' is smart, but it depends on an engineering lead and conflict-resolution details not supplied. Without that source, it is a product blog, not a press angle.

'features that the company says unblocked these pilots' tightens causation slightly beyond the facts. The update ties the features to regulated buyers generally, not specifically to all four bank pilots.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it finds the one genuinely different lever A left on the floor: "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm." That gives the founder a fourth beat and a business-model story, not another compliance wrapper. The compliance angle is underpowered: "Honestly weak as a standalone time hook" is correct, which means it probably should have been demoted unless a live regulatory peg exists.
Slight overreach in "before a competitor matches the feature set" because no competitor status or timing is in the update.

gaps_in_A: "Duolingo says people are talking to its cartoon owl" is factually sloppy: the update says users talk with Lily, not the owl. Cute headline, wrong character.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to stop at four real stories and keep each one closer to what can actually be proved. Next step says '`meanest-editor`' before building a journalist list. For angle selection, the sharper next move is fit-checking reporters after proof gaps are answered.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it is the steadier press instrument: it keeps the launch facts in view and tells the founder exactly what proof would make each lane real. verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives a founder more usable routes to different reporters, not just cleaner labels on the same launch. "Duolingo Lets Subscribers Talk to an AI. verdict.rationale: B wins because its angles are cleaner, fewer, and more alive to an actual editor: “Duolingo's paid subscribers can now video-call an AI cartoon to practice speaking” is a story, not a taxonomy exercise. verdict.rationale: A wins because it mostly keeps its hands on the supplied facts and turns them into usable newsroom lanes. gaps_in_A: "it lands on 4 million desks" treats total users as guaranteed exposure. The update gives user count, not activation, eligibility, or Make availability.
"What that means for the people who used to draw it" leans toward replacement before the facts prove replacement. The update says prompt-generated layouts, not displaced designers.

"Figma's standalone answer is AI code export" is a little too declarative for the Adobe-collapse angle. A correctly flags the missing collapse date, but that uncertainty should probably demote the angle unless timing is fresh.
gaps_in_B: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overclaims the competitive set. The facts say design-file export plus prompt-generated layouts, not a full prompt-to-app market entry.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is invented market context. Maybe true, maybe not; from this update, it is newsroom contraband.
"Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" is puffed-up strategy narration with no supplied scale, roadmap, or executive framing behind it.
"Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice" assumes paid enterprise adoption from a usage claim. "Used at most Fortune 500 companies" is not the same as "these teams will buy the add-on."

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest technical story closer to the supplied facts: 'Figma Make turns design files into React — and squeezes the designer-developer handoff' is testable without pretending the code is production-ready. B is almost there, but 'Figma turns designs into shippable React code' commits the exact sin its own proof section warns against. Both sets overreach on the Adobe peg, but A's proof asks are cleaner and its refused angles are sharper founder medicine.
gaps_in_A: 'Figma's first big swing since the Adobe deal died' is not in the fact block. The update says the launch follows the collapse, not that this is Figma's first major post-deal move.

'a whole job boundary — is what's being automated' pushes the labor-impact claim harder than the facts support. Good angle, but it needs adoption or code-quality evidence before that sentence earns its lunch.

'buyer-side reporter can do math on' the 4M users and Fortune 500 claims risks implying paid-seat adoption from legacy company-stated metrics. A flags the source, but the math still needs a narrower buyer base.
The product/category angle misses competitor context. A skeptical dev-tools reporter will ask how Make compares with existing design-to-code tools before buying the category story.
gaps_in_B: 'Figma turns designs into shippable React code' overclaims. The supplied fact is 'working front-end code'; shippable is a production-quality claim B has not earned.

'Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died: ship, not sell' is too cute and unsupported. The fact block says the launch follows the Adobe collapse, not that it is the first move or a strategic response.

'category-creation' is inflated without competitor evidence. B later admits this with 'How does the generated code and design-to-code claim compare to existing tools,' but the headline frame still outruns the proof.
'first notable product push after the collapse' repeats the same unsupported Adobe-sequencing claim in the body. Caveating it later does not un-invent it.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable newsroom strategy, not just cleaner summaries: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" is a risky headline, but it opens a real enterprise procurement and security lane and then names the proof that would make or kill it. B has solid work, especially "Figma puts a price on AI: a new $25-a-month seat on top of existing plans," but its lead angle leans on "first big swing" and "bet on staying independent," both bigger than the supplied facts. A has its own overreach, but it exposes the hard proof gates instead of hiding behind tidy three-angle safety.
gaps_in_A: "first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" is not in the fact block. Post-Adobe is fair; first/substantive needs verification.
"The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" overstates "working front-end code" into production code before any customer has shipped it.
"Design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" may be useful context, but it is not supplied here and needs sourcing.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is too indirect for a live launch. The practical next move is fit-checking reporters once the proof gaps are answered.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died" and "first major move" are invented unless someone verifies Figma has not made other major moves since the deal collapsed.
"a bet on staying independent" turns "no IPO timing disclosed" into a strategy claim. That is a nice narrative until a reporter asks who said it.
"A customer-story angle — `no_journalist_shape` as supplied" throws away a real enterprise-procurement angle. The problem is missing proof, not missing beat shape.
"clarity on exactly who needs a Make seat" is necessary but thin. The pricing angle also needs attach-rate, budget-owner, and bundling answers or it is just a price tag with adjectives removed.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds the extra real newsroom lane B leaves on the table: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" turns the adoption claim into an enterprise procurement and security story with a hard proof gate. B is strong, but "Figma turns designs into shippable React code — moving onto the developers' turf" is the obvious dev-tools angle, and its pricing/corporate angles mostly stay in the first ring of the announcement. Both overplay the post-Adobe timing, but A is more useful to a founder because its proof demands are sharper and its angles cover more genuinely different buyers.
gaps_in_A: "The launch is the first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" invents "first" and "framed"; the update only says the launch follows the collapsed deal.
"The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" is a useful angle, but "production code" is not in evidence until a customer says they ship or approve it.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is a bit too clever; with a live launch, the direct move is reporter fit-checking once code samples, customer proof, and pricing details are nailed.
gaps_in_B: "shippable React code" overstates the fact block; it says working front-end code, not code engineers would actually ship.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died: ship, not sell" invents "first" and reaches for a cute corporate-saga line without IPO or M&A evidence.
It misses the enterprise procurement story sitting in "used at most Fortune 500 companies" plus generated code; that is a real CIO/security beat, not a footnote.
"any early read on buyer reaction" is too soft as proof; the pricing angle needs seat scope, attach rate, and budget owner, not buyer-reaction mist.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it knows where the floor is. The line "The 4M-user and Fortune 500 figures are Figma's own claims — flag them as company-stated" is boring in the right way: disciplined, usable, and resistant to founder fantasy. A has more angles, including a useful competitive one, but "That's a different company than Adobe would have built" is a counterfactual wearing a trench coat. Breadth is nice; not stepping on a rake is nicer.
gaps_in_A: "first major product announcement as a fully independent company after the Adobe deal fell apart" is not in the update. The facts say the launch follows the Adobe collapse, not that it is the first major post-collapse announcement.
"That's a different company than Adobe would have built" is an invented counterfactual. It may be a sharp question, but A states it like evidence.
"Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io" may be directionally useful, but those competitors are not in the fact block. If the exercise forbids outside invention, this needs sourcing or removal.
"without disrupting its existing base" overreads the $25 seat. The update says the seat sits on top of existing plans; it does not prove the buyer impact or strategy.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died" and "first major move" repeat the same unsupported leap A makes. The update gives sequence, not rank or significance.
B wrongly tosses "Design tool becomes dev tool: Figma enters the code-generation category" as a duplicate. Competitive-market impact is not the same story as designer-developer handoff.
"what does Figma do now that the exit is gone" assumes the Adobe deal should be framed as an exit. Plausible, but not supplied, and it needs care.
"a whole job boundary — is what's being automated" is a little too hot without output-quality or adoption proof. The proof section catches it, but the angle headline still leans past the evidence.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it turns the same launch into sharper assignment desks, especially enterprise procurement: "The Fortune 500 design tool is now asking to write production code" gives a CIO-trade reporter an actual problem to report, even if the proof bar is high. A is sturdy, but "Post-Adobe, Figma's First Major Launch" smuggles in a "first major" claim the update never gave it and spends too much energy explaining why the angles are distinct. B still needs a facts diet; it won on reporter-usefulness, not clean grounding.
gaps_in_A: "Figma's First Major Launch" and "first major product announcement" are invented. The update says the launch follows the Adobe collapse; it does not say this is Figma's first major anything.
"That's a different company than Adobe would have built" is boardroom fan fiction without a quote, document, or analyst source in the update.
"Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io" may be plausible category context, but none of those competitors appear in the supplied facts. Verify before making them the spine of a pitch.
"Tells You Exactly What Figma Is Selling" overclaims what one $25 add-on seat proves. Pricing is a signal, not a confession under oath.
gaps_in_B: "design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" is outside the supplied facts. It may be true; it is still not grounded here.
"starts emitting code that ships to production" and "asking to write production code" overstate the update. We have React and HTML/CSS export, not evidence anyone will ship it.
"first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" invents both firstness and framing. The update gives sequence, not strategy.
"newsjack-detector" is a muddled next step for a launch-angle set. The immediate job is proof collection plus journalist-fit-check; hunting a bigger peg can wait unless the launch hook is too weak.

verdict.rationale: B wins slightly because it keeps its hands cleaner: it labels what is company-stated, asks for proof before making the big claims, and refuses the IPO bait. A has the sharper extra market lens in "Figma Has 4 Million Users and Just Entered AI Code Generation," but it also wanders into unsourced story varnish like "first major product announcement" and "That's a different company than Adobe would have built." B's "Figma adds a $25 seat for AI design-to-code, on top of what teams already pay" is a plain, pitchable SaaS-pricing angle; boring in the useful way.
gaps_in_A: "first major product announcement as a fully independent company" is unsupported. The update only says the launch follows the Adobe collapse; it does not establish first or major.
"weeks away from being absorbed into Adobe" and "That's a different company than Adobe would have built" are narrative garnish, not supplied fact. Fine as a question, sloppy as asserted framing.
"The $25 'Make' Seat Tells You Exactly What Figma Is Selling Post-Adobe" overclaims the pricing read; the facts give a price, not a definitive strategy.
"no IPO timing disclosed" gets inflated into "a meaningful negative signal"; absence of timing is not an investor thesis without a source who will say it.
gaps_in_B: "shippable React code" is ahead of the evidence. The update says working front-end code; shippable is exactly what the proof has to establish.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" smuggles in 'first.' The facts say the launch follows the collapse, not that it is the first move or first notable push.
"category-creation" is too grand for this fact set. A tool exporting React may pressure a category, but category creation needs adoption, competitor movement, or buyer behavior evidence.
"three structurally distinct shapes exist" leaves out a real fourth shape: Figma's 4 million users and Fortune 500 reach as distribution pressure on prompt-to-UI and design-to-code rivals.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it edits: three real beats, each with the proof test that would make or break the pitch. Its line "Without the code-quality proof this angle gets torn apart on contact" is the adult in the room; A's "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" is punchy but drags in a competitive market the supplied facts did not establish. A has useful material, but it pads into shakier labor and competitive claims where B stays disciplined.
gaps_in_A: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overstates the competitive field; the update gives product capabilities, not a mapped prompt-to-app market.
"dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is imported context, not a supplied fact. If you need that market claim, prove it or cut it.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" piles causality and magnitude onto one thin fact: the launch followed the deal collapse.
"the first time the question has real stakes rather than being hypothetical" in the junior-developer angle is too grand. The update has no labor data, hiring signal, or adoption proof.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died" is still unsupported. The update says the launch follows the collapse, not that it is first, biggest, or explicitly strategic.
"what does Figma do now that the exit is gone" is a loaded corporate-frame leap. It may be true newsroom shorthand, but the facts only say no IPO timing was disclosed.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is premature if no target names exist yet. Build the beat list first, then fit-check names against the chosen angle.
The AI assistant fact is underused. B folds "generates layouts from a text prompt" into the handoff story but never tests whether that assistant is itself a distinct design-workflow angle.

verdict.rationale: B wins because its proof demands are sharper, especially the line under "What happens to front-end work when the design file compiles": "This angle dies without inspectable code." A has useful bones, but "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overstates the facts and invents too much competitive scenery. B still needs a fact scrub, but it gives the founder better go/no-go tests instead of five lanes that tempt a spray-and-pray pitch.
gaps_in_A: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overstates the update; the facts say Make exports from a Figma file and an assistant generates layouts, not that Figma ships a full prompt-to-app app builder.
"the first major product move disclosed after the acquisition's collapse" is not in the update; you only have "follows the collapse," not first or major.
"its biggest bet yet" is headline foam unless you can prove investment size, strategic priority, or revenue expectations.
"automating a specific, common junior task" turns capability into labor-market impact without evidence; the proof section admits the hiring data is absent.
gaps_in_B: "first substantive product move framed against the collapsed Adobe acquisition" invents both "first" and "framed" unless Figma actually said that.
"what Make does that the incumbent's design-to-code tooling doesn't" smuggles in Adobe tooling as a competitive fact not supplied.
"Design-to-code has been promised for a decade and has repeatedly produced unmaintainable output" may be useful background, but from this update it is unsourced.
"Story type: customer-story" under the enterprise angle is mislabeled; it has no customer story and says the angle is dead without one.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it knows where the fact block ends and the pitch begins. Its pricing angle warns that "over 4 million users / most Fortune 500" are company-stated figures and "not used as proof of adoption of this paid seat"; A keeps reaching with "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" and "biggest bet yet." A has useful raw material, but B is the set a founder can act on without accidentally pitching inference as fact.
gaps_in_A: "Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" overclaims the competitive field; the update does not establish a prompt-to-app market, named rivals, or that Make competes with "every" such tool.
"The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet" invents magnitude and motive. The facts only say the launch follows the collapsed Adobe acquisition.

"Figma's new $25 AI seat is a bet that Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice" turns existing Figma usage into implied Make adoption and makes "on top of existing plans" sound like literally paying twice.
"what happens to junior front-end developers?" is a viable question, but A leans too hard on "automating a specific, common junior task" without labor data or a Figma statement.
gaps_in_B: "shippable React code" in the headline outruns the supplied fact "working front-end code." B later asks whether engineers would ship it, but the headline should not assume the answer.
"Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" and "first notable product push" are not established by the update. The fact block says the launch follows the collapse, not that it was first.
B leaves a narrower labor angle unexplored. It rightly rejects vague "future-of-work" mush, but a tightly proofed junior front-end workflow angle could have been usable.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is slightly premature unless real names already exist. Pick the angle, build the target list, then fit-check each journalist.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives a founder five usable roads into different desks and is much more disciplined about what proof would make each one real. Its pricing angle, "Figma's new $25 AI seat is a bet that Fortune 500 design teams will pay twice," is a clean SaaS-business story with the right proof asks: adoption, comps, and customer or analyst reaction. B has real bones, but lines like "a company that was weeks away from being absorbed into Adobe" and "That's a different company than Adobe would have built" are invented confidence wearing a strategy blazer.
gaps_in_A: "The Adobe deal died. Figma's answer was to launch its biggest bet yet." overclaims the supplied facts; the update says the launch follows the Adobe collapse, not that Make is Figma's biggest bet or an intentional answer.
"a market that's so far been dominated by smaller AI-native code-generation startups" is an unsourced market-structure claim. If you want that fight, bring named competitors or soften it.
"Figma just picked a fight with every AI tool that turns a prompt into an app" is too broad. Every tool? No. That is headline heat outrunning the evidence.
"automating a specific, common junior task" makes the labor angle sharper than the facts allow. It needs code-quality evidence and hiring-manager proof before it leaves the room.
gaps_in_B: "first major product announcement as a fully independent company" and "weeks away from being absorbed into Adobe" are not in the update. That makes the post-Adobe hook sound reported when it is partly embroidery.
"That's a different company than Adobe would have built" is a counterfactual dressed as insight. No leadership quote, roadmap evidence, or Adobe comparison supports it.
"Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io" imports a named competitive map the update did not provide. Maybe true, but blind judging punishes maybe.
"no IPO timing disclosed is a meaningful negative signal" overreads an absence. The fact supports not pitching an IPO-timing story, not building investor tea leaves out of silence.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it finds the fourth real story hiding in the update: "Flat prices, rising food costs, undisclosed labor savings: the math behind Chipotle's freeze." A is disciplined, but it leaves that money story as a caveat: "the fact block pairs the two but never connects them." B does nick itself by overclaiming that 100 stores "cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation," but it still gives the founder the sharper strategic map.
gaps_in_A: A underplays the finance/equities angle. It says "the fact block pairs the two but never connects them," which is true, but stops there instead of shaping the skeptical margin story a reporter may actually write.
"Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is plausible beat context, but it is not in the update. It needs sourcing or softer framing.
"100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for" sounds made up. Useful instinct, sloppy authority.

The refused angle "Automation savings let Chipotle protect margins" is rightly killed as a claim, but A misses the cleaner version: ask how the price freeze is funded without asserting automation paid for it.
gaps_in_B: "100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation" is too confident without labor savings, capex, store mix, or food-cost numbers. That is a question, not a conclusion.
"so a year of flat prices is being funded by something else" overstates what the supplied facts prove. Say the funding mechanism is undisclosed; do not pretend the math has been done.
"The reporter can do the arithmetic from the supplied facts alone" is the dangerous sentence. The supplied facts support skepticism, not arithmetic.
"the user's own evidence of food-cost inflation in Chipotle's basket" is a useful proof demand, but the set should flag that this evidence is missing rather than implying it exists.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the three real stories separated and refuses to staple unsupported causality onto them. Its cleanest move is warning that “the fact block pairs the two but never connects them,” which is exactly the discipline B loses when it calls the two-robot setup “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format.” B has usable pieces, but it keeps trying to make the story bigger than the facts will carry.
gaps_in_A: “inflation coverage gives it immediate context” is plausible but still a soft peg; no live inflation story or competitor pricing context was supplied.
“Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory” is a useful beat frame, but it is external context, not a supplied fact.
The price angle could ask harder whether a flat-price pledge applies to delivery, regional menus, portions, and fees.
gaps_in_B: “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” is overclaiming. Digital Makeline is only being tested, and nothing says the two systems interact as one architecture.
“Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it” invents industry reaction. Maybe true, but not in the update.
“Half the prep time: what a guacamole robot actually does to a lunch rush” leans on wait-time and service-speed effects not supplied; it is a proof question, not yet a story.
“Run the detector first” is the wrong next step for a company announcement that already has three pitchable beats; prove the claims and fit-check reporters before hunting for a bigger peg.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it refuses the easy lie. Its best line is the adult in the room: "the fact block pairs the two but never connects them, and a reporter will ask." B has useful instincts, but it keeps writing checks the facts cannot cash, especially "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." That is not framing; that is smuggling causality through the headline and hoping the caveat underneath bails you out.
gaps_in_A: "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is plausible beat context, but it is still an unsupported broad claim. It should be softened or tied to outside proof before pitching.
The set misses a possible investor/operator margin angle, but A is right not to elevate it without labor-cost figures. That omission is discipline, not laziness.
"Decay: 24hr" on the price-hold angle may be too harsh because food inflation and menu pricing have a longer trade/business tail, but the urgency logic is defensible.
gaps_in_B: "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" invents a causal link the update does not give. The set later admits the link is "implied but not proven," which means the headline is already guilty.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is worse: the company did not say that in the supplied facts. You cannot launder an analyst question into a company claim.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" is unsupported color. No competitor reaction or behavior was supplied, so this is headline theater.

The consumer-pricing angle and the investor-margin angle are partially the same story in different shoes: automation as the mechanism for holding prices/margins. One can survive, but not both without harder financial proof.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it has discipline: three angles, three beats, three proof paths. Its price angle is especially clean because it says the quiet part out loud: "do not claim savings pay for it." B has good instincts, but keeping "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" as its own angle is exactly the padding A correctly refused: a metric is not automatically a story.
gaps_in_A: The trend angle overstates the category context with "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" and "100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for"; those may be true, but they are not in the supplied facts.

The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is a little early for the labor and pricing angles. A founder still needs staffing-hours data, price-pledge terms, or an on-record link/no-link between automation and pricing before pitching hard.
A misses the sharper scale-skepticism buried in the facts: 100 restaurants out of 3,500+ is under 3%, which could weaken the "leave the pilot phase" framing.
gaps_in_B: B pads the robotics story into too many envelopes: "guac robot reaches 100," "automating both ends of the kitchen," and "one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" are not three fully separate stories.

"call it a pilot, not a rollout" is a punchy line, but it argues past the fact block, which says Chipotle is rolling Autocado out to 100 restaurants. Skepticism is useful; pretending the supplied rollout is not a rollout is cute and risky.

"Autocado plus the in-testing Digital Makeline reads as a coordinated strategy" overclaims. The update says Digital Makeline is being tested; it does not prove a coordinated kitchen-automation strategy.
"making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" invents timing. The facts say the systems exist in this update, not that this is the first disclosure.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it keeps the rollout's size honest instead of trying to inflate a kitchen robot into a category thesis. "Chipotle's avocado robot goes from pilot to 100 stores, still under 3% of the chain" is a usable reporter spine; A's "Two robots, one bowl: Chipotle is automating the assembly line from both ends" wanders into architecture theater and then claims "first evidence" it does not have. B still has a bad overreach in the margin angle, but its refusals and next step are cleaner founder strategy.
gaps_in_A: "first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format" is not in the update. Digital Makeline is only being tested; no scale, timeline, interaction with Autocado, or industry-first proof was supplied.
"Two robots, one bowl: Chipotle is automating the assembly line from both ends" overstates the fact pattern. One robot is rolling out to 100 stores; the second system is still a test.

"Both the 100-restaurant rollout and the price-freeze commitment are live company news as of today" assumes a public announcement timing from the brief. The current time is supplied, but prior coverage and exact announcement mechanics are not.
"Next step: newsjack-detector" is a detour. The sharper next move is to pick the safest angle, secure the missing proof, then run journalist-fit-check.
gaps_in_B: "100 robot-equipped stores out of more than 3,500 cannot offset chain-wide food-cost inflation" is too confident. Without food-cost inflation size, Autocado cost, labor savings, rollout timing, or margins, that arithmetic is not proven.
"The people who made guac are headed to the counter" narrows "front line" into "counter." Maybe true, but the update does not say counter.
"The prevailing belief is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" needs outside market evidence. Useful frame, but not grounded in the supplied update.
"This beat has watched kitchen robots stall at the demo stage" is plausible context, not supplied fact. Label it as a reporter context to verify, not something the brief proves.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the causal claim on a leash: “The story isn't the robot; it's the pairing” is a real restaurant-operations angle without pretending Chipotle proved the math. B has usable bones, but “Its Avocado Robot Explains Why” and “Competitors Are Taking Notes” sell inference as fact. That is how a decent pitch gets turned into a correction email.
gaps_in_A: “the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” overreaches. The update supports two robot systems, not first evidence or full-line automation.
“the two statements were made together” is treated as established. The supplied update pairs the facts, but does not explicitly say Chipotle announced them together.
“The margin question survives longer” is plausible, but still needs outside market context before it becomes more than company-news analysis.
gaps_in_B: “Its Avocado Robot Explains Why” states causality the update does not prove. The set later admits the link is only implied, but the headline already spent the credibility.
“Labor Advocates Are Watching” invents a reaction. The update says no job cuts; it does not say advocates, unions, or researchers are currently watching.
“Its Competitors Are Taking Notes” is unsupported. No competitor response, analyst note, or category signal was supplied.
“Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices” is not grounded. Chipotle says prices stay flat and robots are rolling out; it did not say robots justify the price decision.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable editorial lanes and tells them exactly what would make each one stand up. Its best line is the pricing frame: “the story isn't the robot; it's the pairing,” which is the whole assignment in one clean sentence. B has useful bones, especially “Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why,” but it keeps leaning past the supplied facts with “call it a pilot, not a rollout” and “the industry's usual pattern of automation reducing headcount over time.”
gaps_in_A: “that's an architecture, and it's the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format” overclaims from two facts; the update says Autocado is rolling out and Digital Makeline is being tested, not that Chipotle has proved a full-line architecture.
“Both the 100-restaurant rollout and the price-freeze commitment are live company news as of today; the two statements were made together” assumes announcement packaging not explicitly supplied.
The category angle could name its own ceiling sooner: 100 of 3,500+ and a separate system still only in testing make this a strategy question, not a proved category shift.
gaps_in_B: “call it a pilot, not a rollout” is a sharp headline, but it contradicts the supplied wording; the facts say Autocado is rolling out to 100 restaurants after pilot kitchens.
“the industry's usual pattern of automation reducing headcount over time” imports an outside claim without evidence from the update.
“Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout, making the two-system pattern visible for the first time” invents timing and novelty the update does not prove.
The next step is too timid: “No clean hand-off yet” underrates the set's own viable angles; a fit-checked trade or labor target could still be built around the stated proof gaps.

verdict.rationale: Set B wins because it treats the causal link between Autocado and flat prices as the land mine, not the headline. A leads with "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices through a year of food-cost inflation," which is exactly the unsupported connection a reporter will stab first. B refuses "Robots are paying for Chipotle's price freeze" and turns the hole into a stronger angle: "Flat prices, rising food costs, undisclosed labor savings: the math behind Chipotle's freeze." It correctly calls "Autocado halves guac prep time" a proof point, not a separate story, while A pads the board with "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half." A is sharper on the rollout skepticism, but B's "Chipotle says it won't raise prices this year, even as its food costs climb" is the cleaner reporter-shaped angle.
gaps_in_A: "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" is too thin as a standalone angle. That number belongs inside the operations or rollout story unless there is methodology, baseline time, and scale proof.

"Chipotle is automating both ends of the kitchen — not just the guac" overstates the record. The facts show one 100-restaurant deployment and one system in testing, not yet a proven kitchen-wide automation strategy.

"Autocado plus the in-testing Digital Makeline reads as a coordinated strategy" is plausible, but still a thesis in search of an executive rationale. It needs confirmation before it becomes a pitch spine.
gaps_in_B: "Food robotics has been stuck in pilot-program purgatory" is an unsupported industry claim. Good line, bad sourcing. Do not smuggle a trend into the room without evidence.
"100 stores is the pilot-to-deployment threshold this beat watches for" invents a threshold. Reporters hate fake precision dressed as beat wisdom.
"Restaurant robots leave the pilot phase" gets ahead of the safer story. With 100 of 3,500+ stores, the better tension is whether this is a real rollout or a pilot wearing nicer shoes.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature for the strongest claims. First nail down price-pledge terms, store-level labor evidence, and rollout timing; then shop names.

verdict.rationale: B wins because its proof demands are sharper and closer to what a real reporter will ask before touching this. B's "What happens to the crew when the guac machine shows up" gets to total labor hours, pay, redeployment, and time-bound promises; A's "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" is a valid fact, but thin as a standalone angle. Both sets overreach on the two-robot thesis, but B wastes less space and gives the founder better tripwires before pitching.
gaps_in_A: "In Chipotle's test kitchens, one robot cut guacamole prep time in half" is a weak standalone story; without baseline minutes, sample size, and commercial-scale validation, it is supporting proof for another angle, not much of an angle itself.

"Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout, making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" adds a "first time" claim the update does not give you. That's how a decent trade angle becomes a fact-check problem.
"company-wide automation thesis" is too grand for two disclosed systems, one of which is only being tested. Say kitchen-automation strategy, not thesis cosplay.
"the industry's usual pattern of automation reducing headcount over time" imports outside context without sourcing it. A labor reporter may know that context; this angle set still has to prove it.
gaps_in_B: "the first evidence that a major chain is automating a full assembly-line format" is an invented bigness claim. The update gives Autocado plus a Digital Makeline test, not an industry first or a full-line proof point.
"Other operators watching this decide their own capex from it" is speculation dressed as market consequence. Maybe true, but not in the supplied facts.
"Two robots, one bowl" is clever, but the angle risks overclaiming integration. The update does not say Autocado and Digital Makeline work together in the same restaurants or workflow.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is tool-brained. Useful only if this is a reactive newsjack; for first-party Chipotle news, the immediate next step is closing proof gaps and checking prior coverage.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous inference in the open instead of turning it into the premise. A's "Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why" is the honest story; B's "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" writes the causal link before the proof exists. B is tighter, but tight wrong is still wrong.
gaps_in_A: "call it a pilot, not a rollout" is sharp but a little prosecutorial; the supplied fact says a 100-restaurant rollout, so the safer frame is scale skepticism, not semantic conviction.

"Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout" and "coordinated strategy" stretch a thin fact. The update only says Chipotle is also testing it; no scope, result, or executive thesis is supplied.
"franchise-manager accounts" is sloppy for Chipotle and not grounded in the update. Ask for GM or store-level manager accounts instead.
"No clean hand-off yet" is too pessimistic. The operations angle around halved guac prep time is already pitchable to a trade reporter if Chipotle can provide methodology or kitchen access.
gaps_in_B: "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" is the big sin. The update says prices are flat and automation is happening; it does not say the robot funds the freeze.
"automation as the implied offset" is still an inference, even if the set later admits it needs proof. Do not put inference in the headline and bury the caveat in the footnotes.
"the prevailing belief right now is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" needs sourcing or softer framing. It may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
"they move to the counter" over-specifies "redeployed to the front line." Front line may mean customer-facing work, but the counter is your word, not Chipotle's.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it treats the causal gap as the story instead of paving over it. Its strongest line, "Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why," is exactly the skeptical frame a reporter can use. B keeps writing headlines that outrun the facts, especially "Its Avocado Robot Explains Why" and "Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices." That is how a decent angle set gets itself sued by reality.
gaps_in_A: "Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout, making the two-system pattern visible for the first time" invents a "first time" claim not supplied in the update.
"call it a pilot, not a rollout" is sharp but a little over-lawyered; the update says rolling out to 100 restaurants, so the safer frame is scale skepticism, not semantic prosecution.
The set misses a clean consumer-prices protagonist; the price angle is framed mainly for finance/QSR margins, not diners deciding what lunch costs.
"No clean hand-off yet" is too restrictive. Some angles need proof, yes, but the scale and labor-accountability angles are already fit for targeted reporter research.
gaps_in_B: "Chipotle Is Holding Menu Prices Flat While Food Costs Rise. Its Avocado Robot Explains Why." asserts the causal link the facts explicitly do not prove. The body tries to caveat it, but the headline already face-planted.
"Chipotle Says Its Robots Justify Flat Prices" is invented. The update says prices stay flat and labor-cost figures are not disclosed; it does not say Chipotle justified prices with robots.
"Its Competitors Are Taking Notes" is unsupported theater. No competitor facts appear in the update, and B's own refused list correctly rejects competitor hallucinations elsewhere.

"Labor Advocates Are Watching" and "investor and analyst reactions will surface quickly" are plausible reporting targets, not facts. B keeps mistaking who a reporter could call for what has already happened.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it keeps the product story alive without pretending the missing proof is already in hand: "Glossier adds three fragrances as it pushes into 800 more Sephora doors" is a real beauty-trade lane. A is strong, but "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is the softer, profile-shaped substitute where the fragrance angle should have been. The difference is discipline: B turns the thin facts into testable reporting questions; A rejects one usable fact and keeps one comfy retrospective.
gaps_in_A: "Glossier launches three new fragrance products" — refusing this outright is too conservative. The first fragrance line extension launching alongside 800 more doors is a viable beauty-trade angle if framed with proof demands, not as naked product news.

"Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" — this is a soft company arc with no named founder, quote, or fresh conflict supplied. It risks becoming the contrarian DTC angle in a nicer jacket.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" — this compresses Sephora at Kohl's into plain Kohl's. The contrast works only if the Kohl's door count is material; otherwise it is a clever headline looking for a spine.

"The prevailing belief is real: Glossier was built as the proof case for direct-to-consumer beauty" — plausible, but it imports market context the update did not prove. A reporter will want receipts, not folklore.
gaps_in_B: "in one step" — the facts say expanding from 600 to 1,400 doors, not that the rollout happens in one operational step. Small phrase, unnecessary overreach.
"Story type: customer-story" — the Sephora at Kohl's angle is retailer-format analysis, not a customer story. The label is sloppy even though the angle mostly works.
"so the launch date is the hook" — no exact launch date is supplied. The safe peg is that the products launch alongside the expansion, not a date you don't have.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it is a little harsher about what can actually be verified. Its angle, "Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see," turns Glossier's private-company opacity into real reporting tension; A's "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is clean, but closer to a profile frame that needs access and history the update does not provide. Both sets are usable; B asks the sharper first-reply questions before the founder can get comfortable.
gaps_in_A: "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" risks becoming a company-profile wrapper unless Glossier supplies principal access and actual inflection points. The update gives a blog origin, not a profile package.
"cult brand's positioning" imports brand-color that was not in the update. It may be true in the real world; it is not grounded in the supplied facts.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" depends heavily on how many of the 800 new doors are actually Sephora at Kohl's. A catches this in proof needs, but the headline is too confident before that split is known.
gaps_in_B: "suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" is a geography and shopper assumption smuggled in from "Sephora at Kohl's." Useful instinct, but not a supplied fact.

"one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" and "the whole generation of internet-native brands" need outside comparisons. B names the proof need, but the angle is already leaning on the cohort frame.

The door-count angle and "Sephora is betting more shelf" may collide in the same retail-trade inbox. One counts the space; the other interrogates Sephora's bet, but they need tighter separation in execution.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the facts load-bearing: "Sephora more than doubles its Glossier footprint to 1,400 doors" is a clean trade story, and the DTC inversion stays tied to the company's own "fastest-growing channel" claim. B keeps reaching for thesis theater: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" and "That's a verdict, not a news item" are not in the update; they are attitude with no receipt. A has four usable routes and knows what proof can kill each one; B has one decent route buried under overclaims.
gaps_in_A: "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is the weakest viable angle; without founder or CEO access, it becomes a dressed-up company history.
"what happens to a cult brand's positioning" leans on brand reputation that is not in the supplied facts. Probably true, but this exercise is not a memory test.
"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" lives or dies on the Sephora-at-Kohl's split, and A correctly asks for it, but the headline is too confident before that number exists.
gaps_in_B: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is invented. The update says DTC-only, not anti-retail.
"That's a verdict, not a news item" overclaims the DTC thesis. One Glossier channel update is evidence, not a market obituary.
"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" and "targets a geographic and demographic profile" invent a shopper story the update does not prove.
The first two angles are padded twins: "trend" and "contrarian" both chase the same DTC-vs-wholesale narrative with only a tonal costume change.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story the facts support and a story the founder wishes the facts supported. Its best angle, "Glossier spent a decade as DTC-only. Wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel," is sharp, provable, and honest about the missing channel data. B has real instincts, but "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" turns concurrence into strategy before the evidence is in, which is how you get a reporter to ask the killing question before paragraph two.
gaps_in_A: Missed a potentially useful fragrance-plus-retail question: it refused "Glossier launches three new fragrance products" correctly, but did not preserve the more interesting angle of whether fragrance needs physical retail sampling.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" needs the Sephora-at-Kohl's split before it is pitchable; A flags that, but the headline still over-centers Kohl's without knowing how much of the expansion is actually Kohl's.

"Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is viable only with principal access; without that, it is a pleasant company arc, not a story. A admits this, but it is still the softest kept angle.
gaps_in_B: "built on saying no to stores" overstates the fact pattern. The update says DTC-only, not that Glossier publicly rejected stores or built its identity on that refusal.
"covering the 'death of DTC' narrative" drags in a market-wide peg the update does not prove. B later refuses "DTC is dead," then smuggles the same corpse into the kept angle.

"Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" depends on external trend proof not supplied; as written, Glossier is being used to prove a retail theory the update does not establish.

"Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" is the right question but the wrong headline. "Times" implies causality; the facts only say the fragrance products launch alongside the expansion.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the fragrance launch where it belongs: mostly refused until there is scent, perfumer, price, category proof, or real positioning. B's fourth angle, "Glossier adds three fragrances as it pushes into 800 more Sephora doors," is plausible but over-sold from the supplied facts; "the category Glossier is using to fill those shelves" turns three unnamed products into a strategy claim the update does not prove. A is not perfect, but "Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see" is a sharper retailer-protagonist line than B's safer shop-in-shop framing.
gaps_in_A: "Glossier is one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" relies on outside context and a judgment not supplied in the update; the 2014 origin is given, but "one of the few" is not.
"suburban strip-mall retail" is an inference from Sephora at Kohl's, not a supplied fact; useful color, but it needs caution or proof.

The trend angle says the protagonist is "the cohort," then admits it needs "one other DTC-native brand's comparable move"; without that, it is a thesis waiting for reporting, not yet a pitchable angle.
gaps_in_B: "the category Glossier is using to fill those shelves" overreaches; the facts say three fragrance products launch alongside the expansion, not that fragrance is the shelf strategy.
"across two countries and two store formats, in one step" may imply simultaneity; the update does not say whether rollout is live now or phased, and B later admits it needs the timeline.
The refused line "From beauty blog to 1,400 Sephora doors..." treats the blog-to-wholesale arc as duplicate, but B throws away a legitimate feature lens that A preserves with the right proof burden.
"customer-story" is the wrong label for the Sephora at Kohl's angle; it is retailer strategy or channel format, not a customer story in any meaningful PR sense.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the best story bounded to the facts: "Glossier's wholesale channel is now growing faster than the DTC business it was built on" is sharp, sourced, and immediately asks what "fastest-growing" means. B keeps inflating the same fact into conclusions it cannot carry: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is not in the update, and "That's a verdict, not a news item" turns one private-company claim into a market obituary. A gives the founder four usable lanes; B gives them one good lane and two headlines that need legal and strategic deflation before a reporter sees them.
gaps_in_A: "LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports corporate context not supplied in the update; if this is source-bound, that belongs in proof, not the pitch shape.
"suburban strip-mall retail" and "suburban America" over-read Sephora at Kohl's without demographic or geography evidence.
"one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" is an unsourced rarity claim; the update only supports the 2014 blog origin and current wholesale expansion.
gaps_in_B: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" invents hostility. The update says DTC-only, not anti-retail.
"The brand that built the DTC playbook" is outside-knowledge framing, and "That's a verdict, not a news item" overstates one company claim into a category conclusion.
"whether the DTC experiment in prestige beauty is closing out" is a fake trend unless backed by comparative market evidence, which the update does not provide.
The first two angles are padded siblings: both are the DTC-to-wholesale reversal with a different hat, not two genuinely separate pitch lanes.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the story bounded to what the update can actually support, then names the missing proof instead of decorating around it. Its strongest line, "Glossier's wholesale channel is now growing faster than the DTC business it was built on," is a real retail-strategy pitch with an editor-shaped tension. B has instincts, but "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" invents timing strategy, says "first fragrance launch" when the update says first fragrance line extension, and turns a usable fact into a correction risk.
gaps_in_A: "A retail reporter covering Sephora and LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports LVMH context that was not in the supplied update. Common knowledge is still not supplied evidence.
"suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora" overreads Sephora at Kohl's. The update gives the channel, not the shopper geography or store-format thesis.

A mostly refuses fragrance. That is right for a generic product-listing angle, but it misses a conditional angle connecting fragrance sampling to expanded physical distribution if Glossier can prove that link.
gaps_in_B: "Glossier times its first fragrance launch to its biggest retail push yet" is the worst offender: the update says first fragrance line extension, not first fragrance launch, and "times" asserts strategy the facts do not prove.
"Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" piles on unsupported framing: "test case," "prestige," and "big-box mall" are not in the update.
"Glossier's whole mythology was direct-only" turns a channel history into brand mythology without evidence. It is plausible, but plausible is where lazy pitches go to sound smart.
"mid-market and suburban shoppers" and "coastal-urban" invent a customer-access geography the update does not supply. Good reporter shape, bad factual footing.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it finds the fourth usable protagonist: the retailer format. "Sephora at Kohl's gets Glossier: what the shop-in-shop deal says about where the brand wants to sell" is not just another envelope around the door count; it names a trade reporter's actual obsession and demands the door split that would make it real. A is clean and usable, but "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" sells the fragrance/distribution connection before it has proof, then admits the two facts may just be sharing a date.
gaps_in_A: "collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is too big for one company's unnumbered "fastest-growing channel" claim; the set flags the missing number, but the framing is still overfed.
"covering the wave of beauty brands extending into scent" imports a trend the update does not supply. Without category evidence, that is decoration wearing a press badge.

"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" makes the product/retail link sound proven before the proof list admits it needs evidence that fragrance belongs on the expanded shelf.
It leaves "Sephora at Kohl's" folded into the scale angle instead of testing whether that format is a separate retail story.
gaps_in_B: "Story type: customer-story" on the Sephora at Kohl's angle is mislabeled. There is no customer outcome here; it is a retailer-format or merchandising angle.
"in one step" implies rollout timing the fact block does not give. B asks for the timeline later, but the argument should not borrow certainty from reporting it has not done.
"where the brand wants to sell" infers intent from door inclusion. Plausible, but still an inference that needs a Glossier or merchant voice before pitching hard.
The Kohl's angle is useful but fragile: "It only stands apart if the Kohl's door count is real and material" is the right caveat, and it means the angle may collapse after one fact check.

verdict.rationale: B wins, slightly, because it keeps the strongest story cleaner: "Glossier spent a decade as DTC-only. Wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel" says exactly what the facts support, while A's "quietly became a wholesale company" gets a little high on its own contrarian fumes. B also has the better proof discipline in the line "Three unnamed products with no prices, dates, or category context is an announcement, not a story." A is strong material, but its DTC and fragrance angles ask the founder to carry more proof than the update currently gives.
gaps_in_A: "quietly became a wholesale company" overstates the fact pattern. Fastest-growing channel does not mean wholesale is now the company's core business.
"the collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is too sweeping without market comps. A notices the proof gap, but the framing still leans bigger than the supplied facts.

"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" is viable only after product names, positioning, and fragrance category context exist. Right now it is a dressed-up product-launch angle.
A treats "Sephora at Kohl's" mostly as a door-count detail and misses the sharper brand-positioning question: what happens when a cult DTC beauty brand enters a more mass retail environment?
gaps_in_B: "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is the softest angle. Without founder or CEO access and real inflection points, it becomes a tidy retrospective looking for a magazine editor to do charity work.
"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" compresses "Sephora at Kohl's" into Kohl's. That headline can mislead if the Kohl's portion of the 800 added doors is small.
"wholesale-led growth phase" overreaches. Fastest-growing channel is not the same as leading channel, especially when the company discloses no revenue or profitability.

The refusal of "Glossier launches three new fragrance products" is disciplined but a little too final. "First fragrance line extension" could be a real beauty-trade angle once product details are supplied.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it found the sharper extra protagonist A left on the table: “Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see.” A’s “A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle” is a softer product-launch wrapper that needs fragrance facts the update does not provide. Both sets are usable; B is just more likely to stop the founder before they pitch the easy-but-thin version.
gaps_in_A: “A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle” treats the fragrance launch as a viable angle without product names, price, notes, perfumer, or category context. That is a product listing wearing a feature hat.
“collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis” overstates what one Glossier channel claim can prove. The set flags the proof gap, but the headline frame still swings bigger than the supplied facts.
A misses the clean retailer-protagonist angle: what Sephora’s expanded allocation says when Glossier itself discloses no revenue or profitability.
gaps_in_B: “suburban strip-mall retail rather than mall-and-city Sephora” is colorful, but the update only says Sephora at Kohl’s. That retail geography is inferred, not supplied.
“Sephora and LVMH’s specialty-retail strategy” brings in LVMH, which is not in the update. True in the real world is not the same as grounded in the provided brief.
“one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc” is an unsupported comparative claim. The update gives the dates; it does not give the peer set.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it gives the founder three usable lanes and keeps the missing proof visible instead of painting scenery on it. A's "The DTC darling that quietly became a wholesale company" is anchored to the real channel shift and then admits, "without a number this stays a claim, not a proven contrarian story." B has good instincts, but "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" and "the one who never made it to the prestige mall" turn assumptions into copy. That is how a smart pitch becomes a reporter's first correction.
gaps_in_A: "collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is bigger than the supplied facts prove; it needs category evidence beyond Glossier's own channel claim.
"Glossier was a poster child for DTC-only branding" relies on outside reputation, not the given update. Plausible, but still not supplied.
"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" makes the fragrance launch sound strategic before the facts show why scent and shelf expansion belong together.
The retail scale angle knows its own hole: "context on how 1,400 doors compares to other prestige brands in Sephora" is necessary before the door count means much.

"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" decorates the Sephora-at-Kohl's fact with an unsupported shopper narrative.
"targets a geographic and demographic profile that standalone Sephora does not reach" is a claim, not a fact from the update. B lists the proof it would need, but says the thing anyway.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its strongest line, "without a number this stays a claim, not a proven contrarian story," is exactly the discipline a founder needs before walking into a reporter's inbox. B has useful shapes, but "Sephora at Kohl's becomes a test case for prestige beauty in a big-box mall" turns one distribution fact into a whole market thesis it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" leans on the blog origin as color, but does not prove why that origin matters to the fragrance story.
"Glossier more than doubles its Sephora footprint to 1,400 doors" treats 1,400 as meaningful before proving whether that is large or ordinary inside Sephora's prestige universe.

"the wave of beauty brands extending into scent" is plausible trade framing, but it is not in the update; A correctly asks for trend context, but the kept angle still needs that support before pitching.

gaps_in_B: "Glossier, built on saying no to stores" overstates the update. The facts say Glossier was DTC-only for a decade; they do not say the brand built its identity on rejecting stores.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it keeps the floors separate: announcement, channel thesis, retailer-format story, product story. verdict.rationale: A wins because it knows where the hard story is and keeps asking for the receipts before selling it. "Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams" mixes users and teams as if they are comparable units. That ratio is interesting, but the wording overclaims the conversion math.

The suggested next step, `newsjack-detector`, is a detour unless there is a specific external peg to hunt. The immediate job is proof: named customer, acquisition identity, enterprise-tier breakdown, and technical guardrails.
