B is cleaner and safer, especially "Can you trust shopping advice from an AI that gets paid when you buy?", but it leaves less behind for a founder deciding what evidence to gather before calling a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" overstates the facts. The update says criticism and legal threats, not that Perplexity was sued.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" is a strong angle but still an inference; A correctly says it dies if referral revenue is shared, but the headline states more than the record proves.

"A multi-billion-dollar valuation now has two revenue lines to defend it" is thin without revenue figures. A admits it is "a topic, not a story," which is honest, but then it still spends a full angle on it.
gaps_in_B: "after months of legal threats" invents duration. The update gives legal threats, not months.
B misses the nastiest publisher-economics question: whether a cited product review that drives a purchase shares in referral fees or only ad revenue.
"A media-business reporter covering publisher economics and the AI-content fight" is serviceable, but B is less surgical on outlet type and exclusion than A.
The refused angles are light; B does not flag obvious bad pitches like competitor-threat claims or SEO/marketing-trade drift.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds the tension inside the mechanics, not just the desks that might cover the announcement. "Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer — and the publisher gets a slice of one payment" is risky, but it names a real economic question and then properly says "if it is shared, this angle dies"; B's closest version, "One AI app, two new ways to take a cut," is cleaner and flatter, like a strategy slide wearing a press badge. A has a bad overreach on "being sued," but its proof gates and uncomfortable questions would save a founder from making dumb calls.
gaps_in_A: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" overstates the record. The update says criticism and legal threats, not an active lawsuit.
"those same publishers" is not proven. No publisher is named as enrolled, and no former legal adversary is confirmed participating.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" is a headline ahead of the facts. The set later admits the referral/ad-revenue relationship needs confirmation, which is good discipline, but the angle title still asserts too much.

"A multi-billion-dollar valuation now has two revenue lines to defend it" is the thinnest angle. Without revenue materiality, round details, or an investor on record, this is closer to a reported question than a story.
gaps_in_B: "One AI app, two new ways to take a cut" mostly repackages the shopping and publisher angles. It is defensible, but the distinct angle is mushier than the headline thinks.
"there is no story until a real number exists" throws away a useful accountability angle. The missing payout number is not just a blocker; it can be the story if framed as arithmetic and opacity.

"which merchants or product categories are live at launch; the referral-fee structure..." misses the sharper consumer-trust proof: whether product ranking is influenced by referral fees and how that is disclosed.

"What Perplexity's multi-billion valuation says about the AI bubble" is rightly refused, but B never rebuilds the narrower defensible version: whether these two revenue lines do any work against the valuation. That is a missed business-press angle, not a hallucination if handled carefully.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it found the sharper fourth story instead of repainting the first one. Its "Can you trust shopping advice from an AI that gets paid when you buy?" is a clean user-incentive angle with a different protagonist, beat, and proof burden; A's "Perplexity Says It's Sharing Revenue With Publishers. It Won't Say How Much." is mostly the publisher-fight angle wearing a darker jacket. A also takes a few sloppy liberties with the record; B has one bad invented word, but it mostly keeps its hands where the facts can see them.
gaps_in_A: "for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is an invented market claim. The update says Perplexity is launching in-app shopping; it does not prove category firstness.
"publishers and their legal teams will need to respond publicly" overstates the consequence. They may respond, but the update does not force a public legal reaction.
"publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" is not established by the update. That turns a fair question into a factual claim.

"Perplexity Says It's Sharing Revenue With Publishers. It Won't Say How Much." duplicates the first publisher/legal-threat angle. Opacity is a reporting hook inside that story, not enough of a new angle by itself.
gaps_in_B: "after months of legal threats" invents duration. The update says Perplexity has faced criticism and legal threats; it does not say months.
"live criticism and legal threats" may be true, but the update only says Perplexity has faced them. Don't quietly upgrade historical context into current active conflict.
"which merchants and product categories are live at launch" is the right proof ask, but without any named merchant in the update the commerce angle needs that caveat kept loud.
The publisher angle still needs one enrolled publisher on record. B says that clearly, but without it this remains a defensive company announcement, not a fully pitchable story.

verdict.rationale: B wins by being more surgically useful: "The AI answer box becomes a checkout counter" gives a reporter a sharper commerce frame than A's broader "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon," which drags in competitors the update did not supply. B also finds a real extra data angle in "What 'hundreds of millions of queries a month' is worth to a publisher, exactly." The bill comes due on grounding: B's "starts paying publishers it was being sued over" is sloppy because the facts say legal threats, not lawsuits, but its proof gates are honest enough to keep the set ahead by a nose.
gaps_in_A: "for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is not supported by the update. Big categorical firsts need proof, not vibes.

"Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" overreaches. Google and Amazon are plausible context, but neither appears in the supplied facts and no competitive response or share data is provided.
"publishers and their legal teams will need to respond publicly" assumes a reaction timeline the update does not establish.

gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" is wrong on the supplied facts. The update says criticism and legal threats, not active lawsuits.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" asserts the answer before the reporting. The set later admits the angle dies if referral revenue is shared, which means the headline is too confident.
"the referral-fee pool apparently is not" is a useful suspicion, but still an inference. It belongs under the question to verify, not as the spine of a pitch until confirmed.
"first visible consumer-revenue mechanisms" is not in the update. Maybe true, maybe not; don't make a private-company revenue-history claim without sourcing it.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the four corners of the facts and does not get drunk on Big Tech cosplay. Its best line, "One AI app, two new ways to take a cut," turns the update into a real business-model story without pretending we have numbers we do not. A has good bones, but "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" is exactly the kind of invented competitor frame that gets a founder over-pitched and then ignored.
gaps_in_A: "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" invents a direct competitive frame the update does not provide. Google and Amazon are plausible calls for context, not facts in the announcement.
"for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is an unsupported absolute. One lazy "first" and the whole angle starts smelling like launch copy.
"publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" is not in the supplied facts. It may be true, but this judge only gets the update, not vibes.

The publisher counterposition and "It Won't Say How Much" angles are both useful, but they partially cannibalize each other; the opacity angle is strongest as the hard edge of the publisher story unless you can prove rejection or bad terms.
gaps_in_B: "beyond subscriptions" is not in the update. Small overreach, but still an overreach; do not smuggle in business-model context unless the source gives it to you.

"Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting" compresses a messy legal backdrop into a neat reversal. It works as a headline, but the proof burden is high: are the same publishers actually involved?

The set is a little too quick to refuse "The publisher-payout angle: how much will publishers actually earn?" The undisclosed payout is not just proof-it-needs; with a critical media-accountability reporter, the missing number can be the story.
The commerce angle needs one sharper stakeholder: merchant, retailer, affiliate network, or shopper behavior. "shopping surface" is clean, but still a little abstract.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper, more press-shaped risk in the launch: "Can you trust shopping advice from an AI that gets paid when you buy?" That is a clean consumer-accountability story A missed while spending a whole slot on "Perplexity won't say how much publishers actually get paid," which is mostly a reporting hook inside the publisher-conflict angle. A has real material, but "same ones it's now offering to pay" overstates the facts; B needs to delete "after months," but its set is cleaner and more useful.
gaps_in_A: "The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" assumes the legally threatening publishers are eligible for, or being offered, the program. The update does not prove that.
"subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is outside the supplied facts. It may be true, but this exercise does not give you that fact for free.

The monetization cluster gets padded: "tests how AI search actually makes money," "receipts its last valuation is betting on," and "real shopping channel" are related enough that they need sharper separation or one should go.
It misses the clean consumer-accountability angle created by the referral fee: whether paid shopping recommendations compromise trust. That is not a side issue; it is the obvious skeptical question.
gaps_in_B: "after months of legal threats" invents a timeframe. The update says Perplexity faced criticism and legal threats, not how long they lasted.
"company accused of taking publisher content" is sharper than the supplied wording. Tie it to the actual criticism and legal threats before putting that in front of a reporter.
"plans to pay for itself" still risks investor fog unless Perplexity provides at least one number. The set admits this, but the headline should not outrun the proof.
It under-develops the query-volume math: "hundreds of millions of queries" could support a standalone commercial-intent and conversion test, not just background color.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it does the thing founders hate and reporters need: it says which angles die without terms. A's "Perplexity's shopping and publisher-payout launch tests how AI search actually makes money" is clean but a little boardroom-safe; B's "Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" is riskier, sharper, and comes with the kill switch that it must not be pitched without confirmation. That said, B needs a lawyerly cleanup before anyone sends it: "being sued over" is not a flourish, it's an unsupported legal claim.
gaps_in_A: "The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overstates the record. The update says publisher criticism and legal threats exist; it does not say those exact publishers are eligible, participating, or being paid.
"subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" imports an outside industry claim that was not in the supplied facts. It may be true, but this exercise did not give it to you.

"Perplexity's new revenue streams are the receipts its last valuation is betting on" assumes the valuation thesis is tied to these launches. A correctly asks for investor proof, but the headline is ahead of the evidence.
A misses the nastiest economics question B catches: whether publisher-cited shopping answers generate referral fees that publishers do not share in.
gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" is too legally sloppy. The update says criticism and legal threats, not filed lawsuits.

"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" is a strong angle but an unproven headline. B handles this well in the proof section, but the top line should be conditional until referral-revenue treatment is confirmed.
"first visible consumer-revenue mechanisms" is not in the update. Perplexity may have other revenue lines; don't invent chronology because the sentence sounds tidy.
"whether it's an attempt to settle out of court with product features" risks implying motive or settlement posture not in evidence. Fine as a reporter question, dangerous as pitch framing.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to keep three real shapes and make the missing proof painfully explicit. Its strongest line, "Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting," is the cleanest newsroom conflict here, and it immediately asks for named enrolled publishers and payout mechanics. A is useful, but "Perplexity's new revenue streams are the receipts its last valuation is betting on" starts dressing a thin investor thesis in a sharper suit than the facts earned.
gaps_in_A: "The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overclaims the facts; the update does not say the threatening publishers are eligible, enrolled, or being paid.
"subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is outside the supplied update. It may be true context, but this exercise demanded traceable facts.
"Perplexity's new revenue streams are the receipts its last valuation is betting on" turns a recent valuation into an investor thesis without an investor, round detail, or revenue evidence.

"Perplexity won't say how much publishers actually get paid" is a fair tension, but as a standalone angle it overlaps hard with the publisher-conflict story unless there is publisher reaction or a comparable deal benchmark.
gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting" still asserts the critic publishers are the payees before proving enrollment or eligibility.
"category-creation" is a little inflated for a shopping launch with no merchants, categories, fee structure, or transaction data disclosed.
"there is no story until a real number exists" is too absolute; undisclosed payout terms can be a legitimate accountability angle if paired with publisher reaction or comparable deal terms.
It underuses the valuation fact. Refusing an "AI bubble" take is correct, but a tighter VC/business-model angle tied to the multi-billion valuation could still work with investor proof.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on rails: "Does \"hundreds of millions of queries\" add up to a real shopping channel for Perplexity?" turns the company's vanity scale into a testable retail-tech story. B has sharper elbows, but "Perplexity Moves Into Commerce, Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" smuggles in competitors and market structure the update did not supply. A is pitchable after proof checks; B needs factual cleanup before anyone should put it near a reporter.
gaps_in_A: "subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is outside the supplied update; either source it or cut it.
"The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overstates the fact pattern unless those specific publishers are eligible or invited.

gaps_in_B: "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" imports competitors not in the update and turns a shopping launch into a head-to-head fight without evidence.

verdict.rationale: B wins by being a little less in love with the angle and a little more alert to what can kill it. Its best line is the discipline in “the angle survives as detect-and-respond, not as improvement,” while A’s “now reacts to snoring by changing the bed’s temperature” is punchier but edges closer to an unproven causal claim. Both sets are real strategic material; B is just cleaner about the traps before a reporter finds them first.
gaps_in_A: “now reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature” overstates the supplied fact unless Eight Sleep can prove the adjustment is triggered by snoring, not merely happening alongside sensing.
“a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response” needs proof before it belongs in the angle; the update did not specify that low oxygen triggers the bed action.

“The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier” is sharp, but the strongest consumer-rights version depends on whether existing owners already have the sensors. A flags this, but the headline reads more settled than the facts.
A misses B’s sharper audience mismatch question: Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers, but snoring and SpO2 anxiety may point to a different buyer.
gaps_in_B: “This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it” is vivid, but still assumes a real-time snoring-triggered response that the update does not fully spell out.
“The question exists the moment the reading appears on a customer's phone” invents the phone/app surface. Probably true, still not in the supplied facts.
“Here is what it is measuring” promises study specifics the update does not provide; the proof section walks it back, but the headline is ahead of the evidence.

“The product costs several thousand dollars. Eight Sleep is privately held” are true facts, but the privately held point is decorative in the subscription angle unless tied to pricing opacity, margins, or investor pressure.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds the cleanest, most grounded product story in the update: "Eight Sleep's mattress cover now reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature." B inexplicably refuses that lane as "Feature mechanics with no protagonist" and replaces it with "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic," which starts importing CPAP incumbents and category power-balance drama the update did not give us. A is sharper because its four protagonists are genuinely different: product mechanism, regulator, paying owner, clinic.
gaps_in_A: "detects snoring or a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response" slightly overstates the mechanism unless Eight Sleep can prove temperature changes are triggered by both signals, not just adjusted automatically alongside sensing.

"existing owner being asked to pay again" is a strong paywall frame, but it depends on proof that existing covers physically contain the sensors; A does flag this, but the angle leans on it before verification.
The clinic-study angle is honest, but "whether its data means anything" needs an investigator or protocol fast; without that, it is still more sidebar than story.
gaps_in_B: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" is too cute and not grounded; the update says a sleep clinic study is ongoing, so the 'before the clinic' contrast is muddy at best.

"where CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors own the snoring-and-oxygen territory" imports a competitive landscape not supplied in the update. That is exactly how an angle gets dressed up past the facts.
"it isn't cleared to say the word" overreaches. The update says wellness, not FDA-cleared diagnostics; it does not establish what words Eight Sleep can or cannot use.

Refusing "Why the automatic temperature adjustment is a breakthrough for sleep quality" as "Feature mechanics with no protagonist" throws away the most concrete launch-day mechanism. The fix was to make the bed's closed-loop behavior the protagonist, which A did.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps finding real conflicts inside the supplied facts instead of decorating them. Its line, "The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier," is a clean consumer-tech story with proof holes named honestly. B has usable bones, but "Your mattress now watches your blood oxygen. Doctors have questions" is padded with unsupplied apnea prevalence, wrist-device controversy, and fake price precision.
gaps_in_A: "Eight Sleep's bed now tracks the same signals doctors use to screen for sleep apnea" leans on a medical framing not explicitly supplied; it is likely useful, but it needs backup before becoming the spine of a health pitch.
"the protagonist is the existing owner being asked to pay again" assumes an existing-owner conflict before confirming whether current covers already have the sensors or require new hardware.
gaps_in_B: "sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed" imports a prevalence claim not supplied in the update.
"On a $3,000 mattress" invents fake precision from the provided fact that the product costs several thousand dollars.
"consumer health companies routinely commission studies designed to validate features rather than test them" is a sweeping accusation with no support in the given facts.
"the exact fact pattern that draws FDA warning letters" overstates regulatory risk from the update; wellness-not-diagnostic is a tension, not proof of an FDA-warning pattern.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it separates four real stories by protagonist: product mechanism, regulator, paying owner, and clinic. Its strongest line, “The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier,” is a clean consumer-tech conflict with proof requirements attached. B has useful material, but “Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time” is a one-company trend trying to borrow altitude it has not earned, and “For athletes chasing recovery data” leans on audience assumption more than supplied evidence.
gaps_in_A: “detects snoring or a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response” may overstate causality; the update says the product tracks those signals and adjusts temperature automatically, but not exactly what triggers what.
“whether its data means anything” is sharper than the facts can fully support until the clinic study design, endpoints, and independence are available.
The first angle should more plainly warn that the closed-loop story collapses if temperature adjustment is not specifically tied to snoring or SpO2 events.
gaps_in_B: “a live clinical study with an unnamed sleep clinic” contradicts the update, which says the clinic is named. That is a needless factual stumble.
“Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time” is padded category wallpaper; the set admits “there's no broader supplied signal beyond it” but keeps the trend angle anyway.

“For athletes chasing recovery data” assumes athletes would treat SpO2 and snoring as a useful recovery metric; the update only says Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers, not that they want or use this data.

“premiumization of health monitoring” and “health-equity reporter” are a bit grand for a several-thousand-dollar smart mattress subscription gate unless there is access data or affected-population proof.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it turns the launch into sharper accountability stories, not just product-adjacent coverage. "Your bed's health data is behind the top subscription tier" is a real consumer-affairs angle with a buyer consequence and concrete proof list; B's "Sleep trackers tell you that you snored. This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it" is useful but softer, and it leans on a trigger/response relationship the update does not fully prove. Both sets are disciplined, but A gives the founder more hard-edged paths to reporters.
gaps_in_A: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" overreaches; sleep clinics already live in snoring/oxygen territory, so the headline creates a clever contrast that may not be true.
"the sensors ship in the hardware" is stated too confidently before the proof section asks whether the sensors are physically present for non-subscribers.
The counterposition angle imports CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors without supplied evidence; plausible beat context, but not grounded in the update.
The study angle is smart, but it probably should be marked weaker than the others until the clinic investigator is on record.
gaps_in_B: "This bed changes its temperature while you are doing it" implies real-time snoring-triggered adjustment; the update only says the bed adjusts temperature automatically.
"consumer-health or sleep-tech product reporter" is a fuzzier target than the stronger regulatory and consumer-affairs beats; that third angle risks becoming a product review.
"defensive-comment" is an odd story type for the first angle; the substance is regulatory-boundary reporting, not crisis response.
The set is cleaner than it is aggressive: it refuses the incumbent/counterposition path entirely instead of attempting a tighter, better-grounded version of it.

verdict.rationale: Set A wins because it knows the difference between a pitchable edge and a decorated liability. A's "A sleep clinic is studying a consumer mattress - and the results aren't in yet" admits the weak peg and demands protocol, funding, publication rights, and an investigator on record. B's "Your mattress now watches your blood oxygen. Doctors have questions." is sharper copy, but it props itself up with unsupplied medical claims like "tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed."
gaps_in_A: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" is too cute and slightly muddy; snoring detection already belongs to sleep medicine, so the headline needs the clinical-adjacency point without implying a false sequence.

"Here the sensors ship in the hardware" may be true, but the update only says the features are software-gated behind the top tier. Do not state hardware availability as fact until the SKU/tier mechanics are confirmed.
The fourth angle leans on sleep-apnea market implications without naming apnea in the supplied facts. It is defensible as a question, not as a settled competitive story.
gaps_in_B: "low overnight blood oxygen is the primary marker of sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed" imports medical claims and statistics not supplied. That is how a decent angle becomes a fact-checking cleanup job.

"Consumer SpO2 monitoring has been a live regulatory and clinical controversy since wrist-based devices added it" is a fake news peg unless sourced. The prompt gave a launch, not a controversy timeline.
"On a $3,000 mattress" invents a price and even shifts the product from a smart mattress cover to a mattress. "Several thousand dollars" was enough; the extra precision is fake precision.
"the exact fact pattern that draws FDA warning letters" is legal-regulatory saber rattling without evidence. Useful question, bad claim.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds four real doors into coverage without pretending the launch is bigger or cleaner than it is. Its best move is "A sleep clinic is studying a consumer mattress — and the results aren't in yet," which turns weak study facts into a valid accountability story. B has useful bones, but "For athletes chasing recovery data" turns a marketing audience into assumed behavior; that is how a pitch walks itself into unsupported fluff.
gaps_in_A: "Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic" is catchy, but soft on fact: the update says a sleep-medicine clinic study is already ongoing.

"where CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors own the snoring-and-oxygen territory" imports outside market context. Plausible, but not supplied, so it needs to stay framed as reporter-side context, not asserted fact.
"Decay: 24hr" and the other exact decay windows are confident PR judgment, but still a little false-precision cosplay without launch timing or existing coverage evidence.
gaps_in_B: "with an unnamed sleep clinic" contradicts the update, which says the study is with a named sleep clinic. That is a basic grounding miss.

"Beds are becoming health sensors, one mattress cover at a time" is underbuilt as a trend. The set itself admits it needs "other examples" because one product launch is not a category story by itself.
"an audience that already tracks HRV and sleep stages" is not in the update. You were given Eight Sleep's marketing targets, not proof of how those buyers behave.
"find-journalists" is the wrong next gate. These angles are fragile; the next move is proof-first angle selection, then journalist fit-check, not list-building by beat label.

verdict.rationale: B wins because its proof gates are sharper and more useful to a founder deciding what not to pitch yet. Its line, "If there is none, say so before pitching; the reporter will ask," is the adult in the room. A is strong, but "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" turns a marketing audience into a test-market claim without evidence.
gaps_in_A: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market" overclaims from the supplied fact that Eight Sleep markets to athletes and biohackers; marketing target is not proof of a test market.

"The story is what this audience actually does with the data" is the right question, but A keeps the angle before it has a named user or usage data. That is a feature idea wearing a customer-story hat.
"the prevailing belief is 'if a device measures clinical signals, it's basically a health tool'" invents a broad public belief. The regulatory angle works without decorating it.
A refuses clinic puffery correctly, but misses the narrower conditional clinic angle: study design, funding, endpoints, and whether the investigator will speak before results exist.
gaps_in_B: "the moment the reading appears on a customer's phone" invents a phone/app surface not present in the update. Same problem with "what the app tells a user" and "What does the app show".

"A sleep clinic agreed to study a consumer mattress. Here is what it is measuring." is thin now; B says there are no results, then still keeps it as a pitchable angle. That needs PI access and study documents before it earns an inbox.
"category-creation" is grander than the facts support. This is a closed-loop product angle, not proof that Eight Sleep created a category.
"The company markets to athletes and biohackers" is bolted onto the closed-loop angle's facts even though the angle itself is not about that audience. Loose sourcing is how slop sneaks back in.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about what can be pitched from the facts today. Its line, "Before pitching the contrarian angle, line up an independent clinician quote," is the right guardrail for a founder wandering near FDA-adjacent fantasyland. B has sharper proof demands in places, but "Eight Sleep's mattress cover now reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature" states a causal mechanism the update does not actually prove.
gaps_in_A: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" overclaims from the thin fact that the company markets to this audience. Without a named user or usage data, this is a conditional customer story, not an angle yet.
"the same signals ... a clinician uses to flag sleep apnea" may be true, but it is not supplied in the update. The angle needs a softer phrasing or outside sourcing before it leaves the room.

"A mattress that watches your breathing and changes its own temperature while you sleep" risks turning into a feature blurb. A correctly flags the competitor/proof gap, but the headline still leans harder than the provided facts allow.
gaps_in_B: "reacts to snoring by changing the bed's temperature" overstates the mechanism. The update says the sensors track SpO2/snoring and the bed adjusts temperature automatically; it does not prove snoring triggers the adjustment.

"a bed that detects snoring or a low SpO2 reading overnight and changes its own temperature in response" doubles down on the same causal leap. That is exactly the kind of sentence a reporter will ask you to substantiate.

"The conflict is company versus its own owners" assumes existing owners already have the relevant sensors or are being charged to unlock hardware they bought. B's own proof section admits that is unconfirmed.

"earn a place in clinical practice" is too grand for an ongoing study with no results and a wellness, non-FDA-cleared product. The careful version is study design and independence, not clinical adoption.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps its best punches tied to the actual update: "Eight Sleep puts blood-oxygen and snoring tracking behind its top subscription tier" is a clean consumer-affairs story with real proof asks. That is how a decent angle set gets its hand caught in the invention drawer.
gaps_in_A: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" overstates the supplied fact; the update says Eight Sleep markets to them, not that they are the test market or actual users of this feature.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it knows what will survive a reporter's second question. gaps_in_A: "The businesses waiting three days for a payment that clears in minutes" invents the before-and-after timing. The update says faster and cheaper; it does not give three days, minutes, or a corridor benchmark.

The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is premature. Before naming reporters, this needs the stablecoin, partner, launch markets, eligible volume, and comparable cost/time proof.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it gives the founder more real lanes without pretending they are all launch-day pitches. verdict.rationale: B wins by a slight margin because it finds the one extra real lane A left on the floor: "Wise says stablecoin rails are cheaper — the open question is who keeps the savings." verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the missing facts fenced off instead of laundering them into story copy. verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the ambition without pretending the missing facts are facts. verdict.rationale: A wins because it mostly knows where the floor is: it refuses "Customer story — `hallucinated_fact`" instead of turning a missing customer into a scene. verdict.rationale: A wins because it finds a fourth usable protagonist, not just another wrapper: “Wise's stablecoin bet is a public-company signal that regulated crypto rails carry acceptable business risk” turns the listed/profitable fact into a real public-markets lane. verdict.rationale: B wins because it turns the same four obvious lanes into sharper reporter questions. gaps_in_A: "For a profitable public payments company, cutting correspondent-banking fees is a margin story" assumes Wise's unit economics improve; the update says the product is faster and cheaper than correspondent banking, not that Wise keeps the spread.

"One of the biggest cross-border payment networks" is probably defensible, but it is still a ranking claim hanging on one supplied number: "over £30B" per quarter. Needs external context before a reporter repeats it.

gaps_in_B: "which bank fees and float revenue get squeezed" stretches past the supplied update. Bank fees are fair; float revenue needs sourcing or it becomes banker fan fiction.

"SWIFT-rail economics" is plausible beat language, but the update names correspondent banking, not SWIFT. Keep SWIFT as a reporter context, not a factual claim from the announcement.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it is more assignment-ready: sharper sub-beats, tougher proof gates, and a real bottom-rung customer angle. Its best line, "Wise routes cross-border business payments around correspondent banking," is clean and testable; A's competing "direct shot at correspondent banking's toll booth" is good, but a shade more slogan than story. The margin is only slight because B also steps on a rake with "three days" and "minutes," which are not in the supplied facts.
gaps_in_A: "For a profitable public payments company, cutting correspondent-banking fees is a margin story" overreaches: cheaper for businesses is supplied, but Wise's own margin benefit is not.

"evidence of other regulated payments/financial companies doing something comparable" makes the category angle depend on outside proof the update does not provide.
A spots the missing customer problem in "without one, the strongest concrete, ground-floor version of this story doesn't exist yet," but fails to turn that into a conditional customer-story angle.
gaps_in_B: "The businesses waiting three days for a payment that clears in minutes" invents timing the update does not give. The body asks for proof, but the headline has already made the claim.

The next step, `newsjack-detector`, is less direct than `journalist-fit-check` for a company-owned launch unless the team is explicitly trying to attach this to outside news.

verdict.rationale: B wins because it makes the load-bearing proof explicit before the founder walks into a reporter's first hard question: "which leg of the transfer the stablecoin actually replaces" and "a concrete settlement-time and cost comparison versus correspondent banking on at least one named corridor." A is strong, but "For a profitable public payments company, cutting correspondent-banking fees is a margin story" drifts into investor math the supplied facts do not yet earn. Both avoid most crypto victory-lap nonsense; B is simply tighter and more useful under pressure.
gaps_in_A: "For a profitable public payments company, cutting correspondent-banking fees is a margin story" assumes Wise's own margin benefit from facts that only say businesses can move money faster and cheaper.

The payments-infrastructure angle needs the mechanics B asks for: which leg the stablecoin replaces, not just a generic comment from SWIFT or a bank analyst.
gaps_in_B: "skipping correspondent banks" is a hair too declarative until Wise proves which settlement leg the stablecoin actually replaces.

"stablecoin regulation is actively being set" imports an outside news peg not supplied in the update; the region-by-region approval fact is enough.
It leaves a plausible equities/unit-economics path on the table: publicly listed, profitable, £30B per quarter is a markets hook, though it would need hard cost-disclosure proof.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the story close to what Wise actually announced instead of turning missing facts into theater. A's strongest line, "Wise's region-by-region stablecoin rollout is a live map of which regulators are ready for crypto settlement," is a little hot but still tied to the rollout fact and asks for the missing markets. gaps_in_A: "Wise's region-by-region stablecoin rollout is a live map of which regulators are ready for crypto settlement" overstates what the rollout proves; region sequencing can reflect Wise priorities, partner readiness, or licensing mechanics, not just regulator readiness.

"For a profitable public payments company, cutting correspondent-banking fees is a margin story" assumes Wise's own unit economics improve; the update only says payments can move faster and cheaper than correspondent banking.

The category angle needs more than "one of the biggest cross-border payment networks" to become a real trend piece; A correctly asks for comparable companies, but without them this is still mostly a Wise launch.
The missing stablecoin and partner are not fatal in every proof section, but they probably are. A flags the gap, then lets some angles sound more pitchable than they are.
gaps_in_B: "£30B stablecoin bet" is an overclaim. Wise moves over £30B per quarter overall; the update does not say that volume is moving to stablecoin settlement.

"EU MiCA, U.S. stablecoin bills, UK FCA regime, Asian frameworks" imports specific regulatory context not supplied by the update. Useful research directions, yes; grounded angle copy, no.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the cleanest rollout story: "AI tutoring is about to reach a million more public-school students — through 30 districts at once" is a real K-12 adoption angle with scale, timing, and proof needs. gaps_in_B: "What one pilot district saw when students used an AI tutor regularly" is a conditional local angle presented as a kept angle. No district, teacher, student, or district-level result is in the update.
"Khanmigo reaches 1 million students" is refused as "no_journalist_shape," but A shows the missing shape: district AI adoption at 30-district scale. B throws away a usable scale story.
"Donors, not districts, are paying" repeats the same overclaim it later questions. "Free to teachers" is not the same as free to districts or students.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps the angles cleanly inside the supplied facts while still making them reporter-shaped; "Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning — by its own yardstick" is the right skeptical evidence frame. B is useful, but A is less likely to get the founder into trouble on the first reporter reply.

"inside the first classrooms to use Khanmigo at scale" leans on classroom access and named districts the update does not supply. B flags the proof need, but the headline still sells a story that does not yet exist.

verdict.rationale: A wins because it keeps four clean reporter shapes without dressing guesses up as insight. verdict.rationale: B wins because it puts the real story where a skeptical education editor will put it: evidence standards before classroom scale.
